usage: object marker 를 + 마시다 (drink); 차 ends in a vowel so it takes 를, not 을
the verb for letting tea leaves steep; 차를 끓이다 is to boil it
counter 잔 for cups/glasses of liquid; the number 한 (one) comes before the counter
to serve tea to a guest
대접하다 is a polite, hospitable verb for offering food or drink to someone
examples: 저는 아침에 차를 마셔요.
I drink tea in the morning.
Basic habit sentence; 마셔요 is the 요-form of 마시다, which contracts 마시+어요 to 마셔요.
따뜻한 차 한 잔 드릴까요?
Shall I give you a cup of warm tea?
드릴까요 is the humble offering form; note 따뜻한 (warm) modifying the noun directly before 차.
감기에 걸렸을 때는 따뜻한 유자차를 마시는 게 좋아요.
When you catch a cold, it's good to drink warm citron tea.
Real-life advice register; 유자차 (citron tea) shows how a flavor word attaches in front of 차.
nuance: 차 (茶) is the Sino-Korean word for 'tea,' the brewed leaf or herbal drink, and because it is a beverage it must pair with 마시다 (to drink), never 먹다 (to eat) — though casual speakers do say 차를 먹다 colloquially, learners should default to 마시다. The same syllable 차 (車) also means 'car/vehicle,' so only context separates 차를 마시다 (drink tea) from 차를 타다 (ride a car); they are written identically. Unlike English 'tea,' Korean 차 covers herbal and grain infusions too, so 보리차 (barley tea) and 옥수수차 (corn tea) are 차 even with no tea leaves. A common English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 먹다 by analogy with 'have some tea,' but in standard Korean a polite host says 차 드세요 (드시다 being the honorific of 마시다/먹다). Natural collocations include 차를 우리다 (steep tea) and 차 한 잔 하다 (literally 'do one cup of tea,' meaning to chat over tea).

mistakes: Saying 차를 먹어요 in formal contexts: tea is a liquid, so standard Korean uses 마시다 → 차를 마셔요. (먹다 is heard casually but is not the textbook form.)

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 주스 ends in a vowel, so 를 not 을
the fruit word goes directly in front; 사과 주스 (apple juice), 포도 주스 (grape juice)
짜다 means to press/squeeze; for fresh-squeezed juice you also hear 생주스 (fresh juice)
counter 잔 covers both cups and glasses of liquid in Korean
examples: 아이가 주스를 좋아해요.
The child likes juice.
Simple preference; 좋아하다 takes 를 on its object, so 주스를 좋아해요.
저는 아침마다 오렌지 주스를 한 잔 마셔요.
I drink a glass of orange juice every morning.
아침마다 = 'every morning' (마다 = each); the flavor word 오렌지 sits before 주스.
여기 갓 짜낸 생주스가 정말 신선해요.
The freshly squeezed juice here is really fresh.
Cafe register; 생주스 (fresh juice) contrasts with bottled 주스, and 갓 means 'just now / freshly.'
nuance: 주스 is a direct loanword from English 'juice,' written in 한글 to fit Korean sounds (the English 'j' becomes ㅈ and the final cluster simplifies), and like all drinks it pairs with 마시다, not 먹다. Because it is borrowed, it carries no 한자 and behaves like any vowel-final noun, taking 를 as its object particle. A key boundary for learners: plain 주스 usually implies bottled or store juice, while 생주스 (생 'raw/fresh' + 주스) specifically means fresh-squeezed — ordering 생오렌지주스 at a cafe gets you the freshly pressed version. English speakers sometimes over-pluralize or add 'a' mentally ('a juice'), but Korean has no articles, so 주스를 마셔요 covers both 'I drink juice' and 'I drink a juice.' Habitual collocations: the flavor noun always precedes (오렌지 주스, 토마토 주스), and you can count it with 한 잔 (a glass) or, if bottled, 한 병 (a bottle).

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 콜라 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
counter 캔 (from English 'can') for canned drinks; use 한 병 for a bottle
톡 쏘다 is the set phrase for a sharp carbonated bite on the tongue
to put ice in the cola
에 marks the destination (into the cola); 넣다 = to put in
examples: 콜라 주세요.
Cola, please.
Ordering minimal form; 주세요 (please give) is the everyday way to order at a counter.
피자에는 역시 시원한 콜라가 최고예요.
With pizza, cold cola really is the best.
에는 marks pairing ('with pizza'); 역시 = 'as expected / sure enough,' a very natural filler here.
탄산 빠진 콜라는 맛이 없어서 안 마셔요.
Flat cola tastes bad, so I don't drink it.
Real-life complaint; 탄산 빠진 = 'with the fizz gone (flat),' and 안 마셔요 negates with 안.
nuance: 콜라 is a loanword for 'cola,' transcribed so the English 'c' becomes ㅋ and 'la' becomes 라, and like any carbonated drink it takes 마시다 rather than 먹다. It functions as a near-generic term: Koreans say 콜라 for the brown fizzy soda regardless of brand, much as some English speakers say 'coke' generically, though 코카콜라 names the specific brand. A useful distinction is 콜라 vs the broader 탄산음료 (carbonated drink): 콜라 is one specific kind, while 탄산음료 is the whole category including 사이다 (note: Korean 사이다 is a clear lemon-lime soda like Sprite, not alcoholic cider — a classic false-friend trap). Because it carries fizz, the signature collocation is 톡 쏘다 (to have a sharp tingling bite). English speakers should remember there is no article and no plural marker, so 콜라 한 잔 더 주세요 ('one more glass of cola, please') uses the counter 잔, while a can is 한 캔.

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 맥주 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 counts glasses; a bottle is 한 병 and draft is 생맥주
따르다 (르 irregular: 따라요) is the verb for pouring a drink for someone
에 links the pairing; this combo is nicknamed 치맥 (치킨 + 맥주)
examples: 맥주 한 잔 어때요?
How about a glass of beer?
Casual invitation; 어때요? (how about?) is the standard way to suggest a drink.
생맥주가 병맥주보다 더 시원하고 신선해요.
Draft beer is colder and fresher than bottled beer.
Comparison with 보다 ('than'); 생맥주 (draft) vs 병맥주 (bottled) is a real distinction Koreans make.
오늘 같은 날엔 치킨에 시원한 맥주 한잔 해야죠.
On a day like today, you've gotta have chicken and a cold beer.
Idiomatic 한잔 하다 ('have a drink'); 해야죠 = 'we really should,' a warm persuasive ending.
nuance: 맥주 (麥酒) is Sino-Korean, literally 'barley(麥) + liquor(酒),' so the 한자 itself tells you it is a grain-based alcohol; as a beverage it takes 마시다, never 먹다 in careful speech. A core contrast for learners is 생맥주 vs 병맥주: 생 (raw/fresh) + 맥주 means draft beer on tap, while 병맥주 is bottled — bars list them separately, and 생맥주 is often shortened to 생맥. Do not confuse 맥주 (beer) with 술 (alcohol in general): 술 is the umbrella term, and 맥주, 소주, 와인 are all types of 술. The habitual collocation 치맥 (치킨 + 맥주, 'chicken and beer') is a cultural fixture, and 한잔 하다 ('have a drink/one round') is the social ritual phrase. English speakers often default to 먹다 because 'have a beer' feels like eating-and-drinking together, but the verb stays 마시다 (or the polite 드시다); also, when pouring for elders, use two hands and the verb 따르다, a 르-irregular that becomes 따라 줘요.

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 소주 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
소주 is sold by the 병 (bottle); the shot glass serving is 한 잔
따르다 (르 irregular → 따라) + 주다 (do for someone); pouring for others is etiquette
에 links the food pairing; grilled 삼겹살 with 소주 is a classic combo
examples: 소주 한 병 주세요.
One bottle of soju, please.
Ordering form; soju comes by the bottle, so 한 병 is the natural count.
어른께는 두 손으로 소주를 따라 드려야 해요.
You must pour soju for elders with both hands.
Etiquette sentence; 께 is the honorific 'to,' and 따라 드리다 is the humble 'pour for (a superior).'
오랜만에 친구들이랑 소주 한잔하면서 옛날 얘기를 했어요.
I had soju with friends after a long time and talked about old times.
Social register; 한잔하다 ('have a drink') is the natural casual verb for sharing a drink.
nuance: 소주 (燒酒) is Sino-Korean, literally 'burn(燒) + liquor(酒)' — a nod to its distilled origin — and as an alcoholic beverage it pairs with 마시다, never 먹다 in standard speech. It is Korea's most common spirit, clear and served chilled in small glasses, and the social rituals around it matter as much as the word: you pour for others (not yourself), use two hands toward elders, and turn your head slightly away when drinking before a senior. Contrast 소주 with 맥주 (beer) and the popular mix 소맥 (소주 + 맥주, a soju-beer bomb); all are 술 (alcohol). A learner pitfall is counting soju with 잔 only — while a single shot is 한 잔, you order it by the 병 (bottle), so '소주 한 병 주세요' is what you say to a server. Another trap is English speakers calling it 'soju wine' or assuming it's like sake; it is distilled and stronger than rice wine, and the verb of choice for pouring, 따르다, is a 르-irregular (따라요), not a regular verb.

usage: object marker 을 + 마시다; 와인 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so it takes 을 (not 를)
color word in front; white is 화이트 와인, sparkling is 스파클링 와인
따다 is to pop/open a sealed bottle; 와인을 따르다 is to pour it
잔 counts glasses; a bottle is 한 병
examples: 와인 한 잔 하실래요?
Would you like a glass of wine?
Polite invitation; 하실래요? is the honorific '~ㄹ래요?' offering form.
이 레드 와인은 고기 요리랑 잘 어울려요.
This red wine goes well with meat dishes.
Pairing language; 어울리다 ('to suit/match') + 랑 ('with') is how Koreans describe food-and-drink harmony.
기념일이라서 분위기 좋은 곳에서 와인을 한 병 시켰어요.
Since it was an anniversary, we ordered a bottle of wine at a nice place.
Occasion register; 시키다 ('to order') and 한 병 (a bottle) fit a special-night context.
nuance: 와인 is a loanword from English 'wine' (the 'w' sound becomes 와 and 'ine' becomes 인), carrying no 한자, and as a beverage it takes 마시다 rather than 먹다. Crucially for particles, 와인 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so unlike vowel-final drink words it takes 을 (와인을), not 를 — a detail English speakers routinely get wrong. Color and style words go in front loanword-style: 레드 와인 (red), 화이트 와인 (white), 로제 와인 (rosé), 스파클링 와인 (sparkling). Natural collocations include 와인을 따다 (to uncork — note 따다, not 마시다, for opening) and 와인이 잘 어울리다 (the wine pairs well). The everyday counter is 잔 for a glass and 병 for a bottle; when ordering at a restaurant the verb 시키다 (to order) is common.

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 녹차 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 counts cups of liquid; 한 (one) precedes the counter
우리다 is to steep leaves; over-steeping makes it 떫다 (astringent/bitter)
녹차 also flavors desserts; 녹차 라떼 (green tea latte) is another common one
examples: 저는 커피보다 녹차를 더 좋아해요.
I like green tea more than coffee.
Comparison with 보다 ('than') + 더 ('more'); a simple preference sentence.
녹차는 너무 오래 우리면 떫어져요.
If you steep green tea too long, it turns astringent.
Conditional ~면; 떫어지다 ('become astringent') teaches the real taste vocabulary for over-brewed tea.
식사 후에 따뜻한 녹차 한 잔이면 속이 편해요.
A warm cup of green tea after a meal settles the stomach.
Wellness register; 속이 편하다 ('the stomach is at ease') is the idiomatic digestive phrase.
nuance: 녹차 (綠茶) is Sino-Korean, literally 'green(綠) + tea(茶),' so the 한자 transparently names the color and the drink; as a beverage it takes 마시다, never 먹다. It is a specific type within the broad 차 family, contrasting with 홍차 (紅茶, 'red tea' = black tea), 보리차 (barley tea), and 옥수수차 (corn tea); note the Korean naming logic differs from English, since what English calls 'black tea' is 홍차 ('red tea') in Korean, matching the East Asian convention. English speakers should avoid the 먹다 reflex and remember the verb for steeping is 우리다 (not 끓이다, which is to boil); the natural counter is 한 잔.

It is a specific type within the broad 차 family, contrasting with 홍차 (紅茶, 'red tea' = black tea), 보리차 (barley tea), and 옥수수차 (corn tea); note the Korean naming logic differs from English, since what English calls 'black tea' is 홍차 ('red tea') in Korean, matching the East Asian convention.
녹차 (綠茶) is Sino-Korean, literally 'green(綠) + tea(茶),' so the 한자 transparently names the color and the drink.
English speakers should avoid the 먹다 reflex (green tea is a drink, so 마시다).

mistakes: Saying 녹차를 먹어요: green tea is a drink → 녹차를 마셔요 (먹다 is for solids).
Assuming 'black tea' is 검은차: in Korean it is 홍차 ('red tea'); 녹차 is green tea, and the color words follow the East Asian convention.
Describing over-steeped tea as 써요 (bitter) when you mean 떫어요 (astringent): green tea's harsh edge is 떫다, the puckery taste, not 쓰다.

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 생수 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
water is counted by the 병 (bottle); 한 통 for a large jug
sold at convenience stores (편의점); 사다 = to buy
통 counts large containers; 2리터 한 통 is a 2-liter jug
examples: 편의점에서 생수 한 병 샀어요.
I bought a bottle of water at the convenience store.
Shopping past tense; 한 병 is the natural counter for a single bottle.
수돗물 대신 생수를 마시는 사람이 많아요.
Many people drink bottled water instead of tap water.
Contrast with 대신 ('instead of'); pairs 생수 against 수돗물 (tap water).
등산 갈 때는 생수를 넉넉히 챙겨 가세요.
When you go hiking, pack plenty of bottled water.
Practical advice; 넉넉히 ('amply') + 챙겨 가다 ('pack and take along') is everyday usage.
nuance: 생수 (生水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'raw(生) + water(水)' — 'raw' here means untreated/natural spring water sold in bottles — and as a drink it takes 마시다, not 먹다. The key contrast learners need is the three-way split among Korean 'water' words: 물 is the plain general word for water; 수돗물 (水道+물) is tap water from the faucet; and 생수 specifically means commercially bottled mineral/spring water. So you 'drink 물' generally, but you 'buy 생수' at a store. Another near term is 정수기 물 (water from a filter/purifier). The 生 in 생수 is the same 'raw/fresh' morpheme seen in 생맥주 (draft beer) and 생주스 (fresh juice). English speakers sometimes call all drinking water 생수, but if it came from the tap it is 수돗물, and if from a cooler it is 정수기 물. Natural collocations: 생수를 사다 (buy bottled water), counted as 한 병 (a bottle) or 한 통 (a big jug, e.g. 2리터).

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 탄산수 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
톡 쏘다 is the set phrase for a sharp carbonated tingle on the tongue
to add lemon to the sparkling water
에 marks 'into'; a lemon slice (레몬 한 조각) is a common addition
counted by the 병 (bottle) or, in a glass, 한 잔
examples: 탄산수 좋아하세요?
Do you like sparkling water?
Polite question; 좋아하세요? is the honorific of 좋아하다 for asking someone's taste.
저는 콜라 대신 탄산수를 마셔요.
I drink sparkling water instead of cola.
Health-conscious choice; 대신 ('instead of') sets 탄산수 against sugary 콜라.
탄산수에 레몬 한 조각 넣으면 훨씬 상큼해요.
If you add a slice of lemon to sparkling water, it's much more refreshing.
Conditional ~면; 상큼하다 ('zesty/refreshing') is the natural taste adjective here.
nuance: 탄산수 (炭酸水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'carbonic-acid(炭酸) + water(水),' i.e. carbonated water; as a drink it takes 마시다, never 먹다. The 탄산 morpheme ('carbonation/fizz') is the same one in 탄산음료 (carbonated soft drinks), so 탄산수 is unflavored fizzy water while 탄산음료 is the broad category of sweet sodas like 콜라 and 사이다. Contrast 탄산수 with 생수 (still bottled water): the difference is purely the bubbles — 탄산수 has 탄산 (fizz), 생수 does not. When the bubbles go flat, Koreans say 탄산이 빠지다 ('the fizz escapes'), and the lively bite is described as 톡 쏘다. English speakers sometimes conflate 탄산수 with 사이다, but 사이다 is sweet lemon-lime soda, whereas 탄산수 is plain carbonated water with no sugar. A natural way to dress it up is 탄산수에 레몬을 넣다 (add lemon), and the standard counters are 한 병 (a bottle) or 한 잔 (a glass).

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 음료수 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 for a glass; canned is 한 캔, bottled is 한 병
코너 (from 'corner') labels a store aisle; 음료 코너 is the shortened form
시원하다 ('cool/refreshing') is the habitual adjective for chilled drinks
examples: 뭐 마실래요? 음료수 드릴까요?
What would you like to drink? Shall I get you a drink?
Host offering; 드릴까요? is the humble 'shall I give,' standard when serving a guest.
저는 단 음료수보다 물을 더 자주 마셔요.
I drink water more often than sweet drinks.
Comparison with 보다 ('than'); 단 ('sweet') modifies 음료수 to mean sugary drinks.
회의 전에 음료수 좀 준비해 주시겠어요?
Could you prepare some drinks before the meeting?
Workplace request; 준비해 주시겠어요? is a polite '~해 주시겠어요?' favor-asking form.
nuance: 음료수 (飮料水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'drink(飮) + material(料) + water(水),' a transparent label meaning 'a beverage,' and naturally it pairs with 마시다, not 먹다. It is the umbrella term for non-alcoholic drinks — sodas, juices, sweet drinks — but in everyday speech it leans toward soft drinks/sodas rather than water, tea, or coffee; if you ask '음료수 드릴까요?' a host will usually reach for juice or a soda, not plain water. Note the near-synonym 음료 (飮料): 음료 is the slightly more formal/written 'beverage' (seen on menus and labels as 음료 코너), while 음료수 is the spoken everyday word. Both contrast with 술 (alcoholic drinks), which 음료수 excludes. A pitfall for English speakers: 'beverage' in English can include coffee or tea, but Korean 음료수 in casual use rarely covers 커피 or 차 — those are named directly. Habitual collocations include 시원한 음료수 (a cold drink) and 음료수 한 잔/캔/병, plus the store sign 음료 코너 (beverage aisle).

usage: 얼음 ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 을; the verb is 넣다 (put in), not 마시다
녹다 ('to melt'); 얼음 takes subject 이 because it ends in a consonant
좀 ('a little/some') softens the request; 주세요 is the polite 'please give'
깨다 ('to break'); crushed ice for drinks is 잔얼음 or 분쇄 얼음
examples: 콜라에 얼음 넣어 주세요.
Please put ice in the cola.
Ordering request; 에 marks 'into the cola,' and 넣어 주세요 asks someone to add it for you.
날이 더우니까 얼음이 금방 녹아요.
Since it's hot out, the ice melts quickly.
Cause with ~니까; 금방 ('right away') + 녹다 ('melt') describes fast melting.
아이스 아메리카노는 얼음을 가득 넣어야 제맛이에요.
Iced americano tastes right only when packed full of ice.
Cafe register; 가득 ('full') + ~야 제맛이다 ('is only truly tasty when') is an idiomatic 'that's the way it should be.'
nuance: 얼음 is a native Korean word (from the verb 얼다 'to freeze' + the noun-forming ending -음, literally 'the frozen thing'), so it carries no 한자, and unlike every drink in this set you do NOT 마시다 it — you put it in (넣다), it melts (녹다), or you crush it (깨다). This is the headline pitfall: English 'ice' in drinks tempts learners to treat it like a beverage, but 얼음 is a solid object, so 얼음을 마셔요 is wrong; instead you say 얼음을 넣어요 (put ice in) and then 마셔요 the drink itself. Grammatically, 얼음 ends in the consonant ㅁ, so it takes the subject particle 이 (얼음이 녹아요) and object particle 을 (얼음을 넣어요), not 가/를. A near-synonym distinction: 얼음 is ice cubes/chunks, while 성에 is frost on a window and 빙수 is shaved-ice dessert — don't mix them. Useful collocations: 얼음을 넣다 (add ice), 얼음이 녹다 (ice melts), 얼음을 깨다 (crush ice), and at a cafe 얼음 많이/적게 (lots of/less ice).

Confusing 얼음 (ice cubes) with 빙수 (shaved-ice dessert): if you want the dessert, say 빙수/팥빙수, not 얼음.

usage: object marker 를 + 마시다; 식혜 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
달다 ('to be sweet') is the signature taste; the ㄹ drops before some endings (단 식혜)
잔 counts glasses; served chilled with rice grains floating on top
traditionally made by fermenting cooked rice with 엿기름 (malt); 만들다 ㄹ-irregular
examples: 식혜 한 잔 드셔 보세요.
Try a glass of sikhye.
Offering; 드셔 보세요 ('please try [drinking]') uses honorific 드시다 + ~아 보다 'try doing.'
식혜는 차갑게 해서 마셔야 더 맛있어요.
Sikhye tastes better when you drink it chilled.
Serving tip; 차갑게 해서 ('make it cold and then') + ~야 ('only if/must') explains the right way to serve it.
명절에 한과랑 식혜를 함께 내면 분위기가 살아요.
Serving sikhye with traditional sweets at the holidays sets a nice mood.
Cultural register; 한과 (Korean confections) + 분위기가 살다 ('the atmosphere comes alive') is idiomatic.
nuance: 식혜 (食醯) is a traditional sweet rice beverage made by fermenting steamed rice with malt water (엿기름), leaving tender rice grains floating in a cool, sweet liquid; as a drink it takes 마시다, not 먹다 — though because of the floating rice some people half-jokingly 먹다 it. Note the 한자 (食 'food/eat' + 醯, an old character for fermented liquid) and the spelling: it is 식혜 with ㅖ, not to be confused with 식해 (食醢), a completely different fermented-fish side dish from the east coast — a near-homophone (sikhye vs sikhae) but a savory food, a classic native-speaker spelling trap too. The signature taste adjective is 달다 (sweet), and it is always served 차갑게 (cold), especially after sauna visits and at 명절 (holidays) like Chuseok and Lunar New Year. A near comparison: 식혜 vs 수정과 (수정과 is a darker cinnamon-ginger punch with dried persimmon) — both are traditional sweet drinks but taste entirely different. English speakers should default to 마시다 and remember the counter 한 잔; to make it is 만들다 (a ㄹ-irregular verb).
